linkedin_post.body:
We walked in with a 35% trade margin and a label that looked premium on screen.

He picked up the jar, turned it around, and frowned at the ingredient panel.

"My mother buys this," he said. "She does not read 6-point font. She reads the front. If it does not say PURE COFFEE or 70% COFFEE right there, she feels cheated when she tastes it."

He handed it back. "Fix the front. Then we talk margin."

That night we rewrote every SKU. Bold, Purista, Purica, and Prima now say PURE COFFEE — 0% CHICORY in type you can read from across a kitchen counter. Ultra Blend says 70% COFFEE, 30% CHICORY — same size, same prominence, zero hiding.

The co-packer said the new die-cut label would cost more and delay launch by three weeks. We switched co-packers instead.

Since the change, our sell-through at that store doubled in 60 days. The retailer now orders every two weeks.

Front-label rule: if the claim is not readable from three feet away, it does not exist.

Bold: Agglomerated pure coffee. 0% chicory.
Purista: Freeze-dried pure Robusta. 0% chicory.
Purica: Freeze-dried pure Arabica. 0% chicory.
Ultra Blend: 70% coffee, 30% chicory — stated on the front, not hidden in small print.

The label is the only contract the customer ever signs. We honour it in plain sight.

## What does milk coffee mean for an Indian kitchen?

In an Indian kitchen, the day doesn't truly start until that first glass of milky coffee hits the table. It is less about a caffeine delivery system and more about a ritual: the rhythmic pour between steel tumbler and davara to build a thick, caramel-colored crown of foam, the specific clink of the spoon against the rim, the steam fogging up your glasses. We judge the brew by how well it holds that foam and whether the flavor pushes through the milk without turning bitter or thin. A strong, agglomerated granule like Bold is built for exactly this — it dissolves fast and keeps its backbone. If your mornings lean smoother, the freeze-dried Arabica in Purica brings natural chocolate notes that don't get lost. And for the household that goes through jars quickly, Ultra Blend at ₹309 for 100g delivers a familiar, comforting cup at roughly ₹5 a serving. The real trick isn't a secret recipe; it's using water just off the boil, not a rolling boil, so the coffee blooms instead of burns.

### A plain definition

Whatever brought you here, the label settles it. Ultra Blend is 70% coffee and 30% chicory. The other single jars on this page are 0% chicory.

## How do you read the chicory line on the jar?

Flip the jar over and find the ingredient list. If chicory is listed first, that powder is mostly root, not bean. If coffee comes first, you are buying coffee with a chicory accent. Bold, Purista, and Purica show coffee as the only ingredient. Purity Beans prints that line straight, without hiding it in a paragraph of marketing copy. A concrete habit: scan for the percentage or the order before the price. A 50g jar of Ultra Blend at ₹209 delivers a familiar, malt-forward cup that many grew up with; the 100g at ₹309 simply lasts longer. The pure-coffee jars — Bold at ₹239 for 50g, Purista at ₹319, Purica at ₹329 — cost more per gram because there is no filler stretching the weight. If your morning ritual leans on milk and sugar, the chicory note can feel comforting. If you want the bean character to show through milk, reach for a zero-chicory jar. The label tells the whole story in two seconds; reading it is the fastest upgrade you can make to the cup.

Choosing a Purity Beans jar comes down to how you actually brew at home. For a smoother, more aromatic cup with natural caramel and chocolate notes, Purica is freeze-dried pure Arabica — the 100g size is ₹559 and works beautifully in desserts or a slow weekend pour. Purista is freeze-dried gourmet Robusta at ₹509 for 100g; it holds a rich crema and gives a bold-yet-smooth lift that carries through an afternoon slump. ## How do people brew instant coffee in Indian cities?

Walk into any apartment kitchen in Bangalore, Mumbai, or Delhi at seven in the morning and you will hear the same rhythm: kettle clicking off, a spoon clinking against a steel tumbler, the quick swirl before the first sip. Most people start with a heaped spoonful of powder, pour a thin stream of hot water just to wet it, then top it off with boiled milk and sugar to taste. Some swear by the "decoction" method — dissolving the coffee in a tiny stainless cup first so it emulsifies properly before the milk hits it. Others keep it simple: granules straight into the mug, milk poured hot from the pan, stirred fast so a thin layer of foam settles on top. The trick nobody talks about is water temperature — just off the boil, not rolling, or the coffee turns sharp.
